newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: MOSCOW GENERAL SAYS RUSSIANS FEAR NATO EXPANSION.
newsitem.headline: MOSCOW GENERAL SAYS RUSSIANS FEAR NATO EXPANSION.

text.p: The planned expansion of NATO to former Soviet satellites has freightened Russians and may damage Europe's geopolitical structure, Russia's chief of the General Staff Mikhail Kolesnikov said on Wedensday.
Ending a three-day visit to Slovakia, Kolesnikov told a news conference that NATO's expansion plans had resulted in "understandable fears and disquiet" in Russia.
"The expansion of NATO could lead to a new geopolitical division of Europe and could damage the security system in Europe," Kolesnikov said.

Several former Soviet-bloc countries have applied for NATO membership and diplomats widely suggest that the Czech Republic, Poland, and Hungary are leading candidates for an initial wave of the alliance's expansion.
Top NATO leaders have said the alliance would press ahead with expansion plans next year and grant full membership to selected former East Bloc enemies despite Russian objections.
Several countries from the region are expected to be invited to a summit to start accession talks in 1997.

Kolesnikov, 57, who was visiting an international arms fair in the west Slovak town of Trencin, said he had not specificaly discussed Slovakia's plans to join NATO in his talks with leading officials.
He said NATO should concentrate more on reorganising itself to be capable of solving crisis situations and participate more in the security aims of the United Nations.
"Our attitude is principal, but this does not mean we're not seeking new ways of cooperation with NATO," Kolesnikov said.
The general, who has been chief of staff since June 1992, said former enemies from NATO and the Warsaw pact should desist from cold war rethoric "because this the will only lead to mutual mistrust."
He said that Russia posed no threat to the West.
The Slovak chief of the General Staff, Jozef Tuchyna, said while Slovakia's intention to join NATO had not been officialy discussed, neither had the subject been entirely avoided.

"We have declared Slovakia's intention for NATO membership but we are also against the creation of blocs, and this entire situation can not be solved by totally ignoring Russia," Tuchyna told reporters.
Kolesnikov flatly rejected a recent statement by Alexander Lebed, President Boris Jelcin's security adviser, that Russia's armed forces faced a possible mutiny.
"I categoricaly reject this statement, if the situation was such, I would not be here," Kolesnikov said.
